title: 22. Interview: Cache Aside Pattern
summary: Interview Q&A for Cache Aside Pattern — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Cache Aside Pattern interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the cache-aside pattern, and how does it differ from a "transparent" cache?
**Answer:** Cache-aside is a pattern where the application explicitly orchestrates cache reads, misses, and writes: on a read it checks the cache, falls through to the DB on a miss, and back-fills the cache; on a write it updates the DB and invalidates the cache. The cache is a "dumb" key-value store — it has no knowledge of the DB schema, no loader, no automatic behavior. This differs from a "transparent" cache like read-through, where the cache itself is configured with a loader and the application talks only to the cache; the cache transparently fetches from the DB on a miss. Cache-aside is more verbose (every read site has miss-handling code) but more flexible — different read sites can apply different TTLs, fallbacks, or coalescing strategies. Real-world: Netflix's EVCache usage is overwhelmingly cache-aside because each service wants explicit control over miss handling.
**Visual:**
```
Cache-aside (explicit):        Read-through (transparent):
App                            App
 |--GET cache                   |--GET cache
 |--miss? -> DB                 |--miss? -> cache fetches from DB
 |--SET cache                   |--(cache populates itself)
 |--return                      |--return
App owns the logic.            Cache owns the logic.
```

### Q2. On a write, should you update the cache (SET) or invalidate it (DEL)? Why?
**Answer:** In most production systems, **invalidate** (DEL) is preferred over **update** (SET). Reasons: (1) Invalidation is idempotent — `DEL` twice has the same effect as `DEL` once, while `SET` with different values races on last-writer-wins. (2) Invalidation avoids computing the new cache value if no one reads it soon — a write-only key never incurs the cache-set cost. (3) Invalidation eliminates the "stale-then-overwrite" race where a concurrent read fetches the old DB value and writes it back, overwriting the new cache value the writer just set. (4) Invalidation composes safely with retry — if the DEL fails, retrying is fine; if SET fails, retrying may overwrite a newer value. The downside: the next read takes a miss (one DB fetch). Update-the-cache makes sense when the new value is cheap to compute and the next read is expected immediately, or when the miss cost is unacceptable. Most production code uses DEL plus a bounded TTL as a safety net.
**Visual:**
```
Write with invalidate:
DB UPDATE -> cache DEL  -->  next read misses -> fetch fresh -> repopulate

Write with update:
DB UPDATE -> cache SET new_value  -->  next read hits, but races:
                                       concurrent read may overwrite with stale
```

### Q3. Describe the "stale-then-overwrite" race and how to mitigate it.
**Answer:** The race: (1) Read thread A misses the cache and queries the DB, getting the old value V1. (2) Write thread B updates the DB to V2 and deletes the cache. (3) Read thread A finishes and writes V1 back to the cache — restoring stale data that will live until TTL expires. The cache now serves V1 even though the DB has V2. Mitigations: (a) **Delayed double-delete** — after the DB write, delete the cache, sleep for slightly longer than the longest DB read (e.g., 100 ms), then delete again to clean up any stale value a racing read may have written. (b) **Versioned keys** — write to `key:v2` instead of `key`, so a stale read of `key:v1` simply doesn't match the new lookups. (c) **Write-through** — make the writer both update the DB and update the cache atomically, so the read never re-populates. (d) **Short TTL** — bound the staleness window so even if the race occurs, it self-heals quickly. Real-world: Facebook's memcached deployment documents the delayed-double-delete pattern for exactly this race.
**Visual:**
```
A: miss -> DB read (gets V1, slow) .............. SET V1 (stale!)
B:                  DB update V2 -> DEL cache
Result: cache has V1, DB has V2  -->  stale until TTL

Mitigation: delayed double-delete
B: DB update V2 -> DEL -> sleep 100ms -> DEL again
```

### Q4. What is a thundering herd (cache stampede) in cache-aside, and how do you prevent it?
**Answer:** When a popular key expires or is invalidated, every concurrent read misses the cache simultaneously, all fall through to the DB, and all back-fill the cache — turning one DB query into thousands. A viral YouTube video's metadata key, for example, might have 10,000 concurrent viewers when its TTL expires; without protection, all 10,000 hit the DB at once. Mitigations: (1) **Per-key locking / request coalescing** — the first miss acquires a lock and fetches; concurrent misses wait for the result instead of fetching themselves. (2) **Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch)** — as TTL approaches zero, each read probabilistically decides to refresh early, spreading the refresh load over time. (3) **Refresh-ahead** — a background worker refreshes popular keys slightly before expiry. (4) **TTL jitter** — add ±10–20% random variation so keys don't expire simultaneously. (5) **Stale-while-revalidate** — serve the stale value while refreshing in the background. Netflix's EVCache uses XFetch and request coalescing precisely for this.
**Visual:**
```
Without guard:                With per-key lock:
TTL expires                   TTL expires
1000 reqs -> 1000 DB queries   1 req acquires lock -> 1 DB query
DB overloaded                  999 reqs wait -> served from cache
                               DB sees 1 query
```

### Q5. When is cache-aside the wrong choice? Which patterns replace it?
**Answer:** Cache-aside is wrong when: (1) **Strong consistency is required** — cache-aside inherently serves stale data between a write and the next invalidation; use write-through or write-behind for stronger guarantees. (2) **Writes dominate** — every write must invalidate, eliminating the read savings; caching rarely pays off. (3) **Miss-handling logic is complex and duplicated** — if every read site repeats the same miss-handling, read-through encapsulates it in one place. (4) **The cache must be self-warming on cold start** — cache-aside warms lazily, so cold starts see high miss rates; read-through with eager warming or write-through is better. (5) **The cache is the source of truth for some computation** — e.g., a counter that must be atomic; use a write-through counter or a Redis-native primitive. (6) **Cross-service cache coherence is needed** — cache-aside has no built-in coherence; consider a shared cache layer with read-through, or an event-driven invalidation system (e.g., Kafka-backed cache invalidation).
**Visual:**
```
Need                         Choose
---------------------------- ------------------
read-heavy, eventual-ok      cache-aside
strong consistency           write-through
miss-handling centralized    read-through
write-heavy + low-latency    write-behind
periodic recomputed          refresh-ahead
```

### Q6. How do you choose TTLs in cache-aside, and what are the trade-offs?
**Answer:** TTL trades off freshness against cache effectiveness. Short TTL (seconds) keeps data fresh but increases miss rate (more DB load) and stampede risk. Long TTL (hours/days) improves hit rate but tolerates more staleness — if data changes, stale values persist until expiry. The right TTL depends on: (1) **Update frequency** — set TTL proportional to the inverse of update rate (e.g., 5-min TTL for data updated every few minutes; 1-hour TTL for data updated hourly). (2) **Cost of staleness** — financial data needs short TTLs; product catalog tolerates long ones. (3) **Working-set size** — if cache is small, long TTLs cause more LRU evictions of other keys. (4) **Stampede risk** — long TTLs mean infrequent but high-amplitude stampedes. Best practices: add jitter (±10–20%) to avoid synchronized expiry; use refresh-ahead for popular long-TTL keys; layer TTLs (5 min for inventory, 1 hour for product, 1 day for image URLs); and monitor hit rate per TTL class. Amazon's product page uses TTLs from 30 seconds (inventory) to 24 hours (image URLs).
**Visual:**
```
TTL       freshness   hit rate   stampede risk
1 min     high        low        high (frequent expiry)
5 min     medium      medium     medium
1 hour    lower       high       low (rare expiry)
1 day     low         very high  very low (but stale on writes)
```

### Q7. What happens when the cache fails (Redis is down) in a cache-aside design?
**Answer:** In cache-aside, cache failure degrades gracefully: reads miss every time, fall through to the DB, and the back-fill `SET` calls fail silently — the application still returns correct data, just slower. The DB must absorb the full read load, which is why capacity planning must size the DB for "cache-failure mode" not just steady-state. Mitigations: (1) **Circuit breaker** — if Redis is down, stop calling it (don't waste latency on timeouts) and go straight to the DB. (2) **Multi-AZ Redis** — replicate across availability zones so single-AZ failures don't take the cache down. (3) **Database capacity** — provisioned for the failure scenario (Netflix pre-provisions DB headroom for exactly this). (4) **Graceful degradation** — return stale data from a local in-process L1 cache or last-known-good fallback. (5) **Alerting** — page on cache-down so it's fixed before TTLs all expire. (6) **Chaos testing** — Netflix's Chaos Monkey kills cache nodes in production to verify the fall-through path works. Cache-aside's design virtue is that cache failure is a performance issue, not a correctness one.
**Visual:**
```
Redis down:
App -> GET cache -> timeout/error
   -> catch -> go straight to DB
   -> SET cache -> error (ignored)
   -> return value (correct, just slow)

DB absorbs full read load (must be provisioned for this)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Netflix stores user playback profiles in Cassandra behind an EVCache (memcached) layer using cache-aside. After a user updates their language preference, the next read still shows the old language. Diagnose.
**Answer:** Most likely cause: the write path failed to invalidate the cache entry, or the invalidation raced with a concurrent read. Diagnose by checking: (1) Did the write code call `cache.del(key)` after updating Cassandra? If the call was missing or in a `try/except` that swallowed the error, the stale entry persists. (2) Was there a "stale-then-overwrite" race? — a read that started before the write fetched the old value from Cassandra and wrote it back to EVCache after the write's `DEL`. (3) Is the TTL so long that the stale entry will live for hours? (4) Is the cache key correct? — if the writer invalidated `profile:user:42` but the reader reads `profile:user:42:locale_en`, the invalidation misses. Fix: ensure the write path is `cassandra.update() -> cache.del(key)` with the key matching exactly what the reader uses; add a delayed double-delete to defeat the race; bound the TTL to 5 minutes as a safety net; and add a metric that tracks invalidate failures so they're visible. Netflix's actual deployment logs every cache invalidate for post-mortem tracing.
**Visual:**
```
T0: read miss -> Cassandra (gets lang=en) -> SET cache (lang=en)
T1: write -> Cassandra (lang=fr) -> DEL cache
T2: read thread from T0 finishes -> SET cache (lang=en)  <-- stale overwrite!

Fix: delayed double-delete
T1: write -> Cassandra -> DEL -> sleep 100ms -> DEL again
T2: SET cache (stale) at T1+50ms  -> cleaned up by second DEL at T1+100ms
```

### Q2. You're building Instagram's home feed cache. The feed is computed by a backend service and cached per user with a 60-second TTL. During celebrity events, feed computation spikes. How do you prevent stampedes?
**Answer:** For a celebrity event, millions of users refresh their feed simultaneously, and many will hit cache expiry at the same time. Mitigations layered: (1) **TTL jitter** — add ±10 seconds to the 60-second TTL so expirations spread out instead of clustering. (2) **Per-key request coalescing** — for each user's feed key, the first miss acquires a lock; concurrent misses for the same key wait and share the result, so the backend sees one computation per key instead of dozens. (3) **Refresh-ahead** — a background worker refreshes feeds for active users slightly before expiry, so the read path always hits. (4) **Stale-while-revalidate** — when the cache expires, serve the stale value immediately and refresh in the background; the user sees a slightly old feed for one request, then the fresh one. (5) **Pre-compute celebrity feeds** — for top-N users (the celebrities themselves), pre-compute their feeds in a separate pipeline with longer TTLs because their feed computation is expensive and their audience is huge. Instagram combines all of these: jitter + coalescing + stale-while-revalidate + pre-computation for top users.
**Visual:**
```
Layered defense:
  TTL jitter (±10s)        -> expirations spread out
  + per-key coalescing     -> 1 backend call per key per refresh
  + stale-while-revalidate -> readers never wait for refresh
  + refresh-ahead          -> popular keys never visibly expire
  + pre-compute top users  -> expensive feeds pre-computed off-peak
```

### Q3. Amazon's product detail page has 8 cache lookups per page (title, price, images, inventory, reviews, related, A/B test, personalization). Cache-aside is used. How do you minimize tail latency?
**Answer:** Eight sequential cache lookups at 0.5 ms each = 4 ms, plus serialization and application logic — fine for a 200 ms budget but risky if any lookup has a tail-latency spike. Minimize tail: (1) **Parallel lookups** — issue all 8 `MGET` or pipelined Redis commands in one round-trip instead of 8 sequential ones (Redis pipelining or `MGET` for same-shard keys; for cross-shard, use a client that fans out in parallel). (2) **Hedged requests** — for the slowest lookup, issue a second request after a threshold (e.g., 5 ms) and use whichever returns first (Google's Jeffrey Dean pattern). (3) **Bound timeouts** — each cache lookup has a 10 ms timeout; on timeout, fall through to a degraded response (skip reviews, show generic personalization) rather than blocking the page. (4) **Co-locate cache** — Redis in the same AZ as the application, ideally on the same rack, to minimize network latency. (5) **Tiered cache** — small in-process L1 cache for ultra-hot keys (image URLs, A/B assignments) absorbs the bulk of lookups without crossing the network. (6) **Pre-aggregate** — store a single composite object (`product:42:composite`) with all the per-product fields, so one lookup fetches everything.
**Visual:**
```
Sequential (slow):          Parallel (fast):
GET -> 0.5ms                MGET k1..k8 -> 0.5ms (1 RTT)
GET -> 0.5ms                + pipeline / fan-out
...                         + hedged on slowest
GET -> 0.5ms
total = 4ms                 total = 0.5ms
+ tail amplification        + bounded tail
```

### Q4. Your cache-aside implementation has a 95% hit rate but the database is still overloaded during peaks. Why?
**Answer:** At 95% hit rate, the DB sees 5% of read traffic — but if peak read QPS is 100,000, that's still 5,000 DB qps, which may exceed DB capacity. Several causes: (1) **Stampede amplification** — when hot keys expire, the 5% miss rate momentarily spikes to 50%+ for a few seconds, overwhelming the DB even though the average is 5%. (2) **Write invalidations** — every write triggers a miss on the next read; during heavy write periods (e.g., flash sale inventory updates), misses spike. (3) **DB capacity is sized for average, not peak** — if peak DB qps is 5× average, even 5% miss rate at peak may exceed provisioned capacity. (4) **Connection pool exhaustion** — the DB has plenty of CPU but the connection pool maxes out at 100, blocking new queries. (5) **Long-tail queries** — the misses that do reach the DB happen to be expensive (full-table scans, joins) rather than simple point lookups. Diagnose with metrics: miss rate over time (look for spikes), DB qps vs provisioned, query latency percentiles, connection pool wait time. Fixes: increase cache hit rate to 99%+, add stampede protection, add DB read replicas, or pre-warm hot keys during peaks.
**Visual:**
```
Average miss rate: 5%       Peak miss rate: 25% (stampede)
Average DB qps: 1,000       Peak DB qps: 25,000 (capacity: 5,000)
                            ^^^^^^^^^^^^ overloaded at peak

Fix: target 99% hit rate + stampede guard -> peak DB qps drops to 1,000
```

### Q5. Uber's driver location is updated every 4 seconds by drivers and read every 2 seconds by riders. Cache-aside seems wrong here. Why, and what would you use instead?
**Answer:** Cache-aside is wrong for driver location because: (1) The read:write ratio is only ~2:1 (read every 2s, write every 4s) — too low for caching to amortize the invalidation cost. (2) Every write must invalidate the cache, which means the cache is almost always cold — the next read misses, hits the DB, and back-fills, only to be invalidated again 4 seconds later. (3) Driver location must be fresh — a 30-second-old location is useless for dispatch — so TTL must be very short, which kills hit rate. (4) The DB writes are frequent (millions of drivers × every 4 seconds), and invalidations add to that write load. Better patterns: (a) **Write-through** — driver writes go to the cache (Redis) and the DB simultaneously; reads always hit the cache (which is always fresh). (b) **Geospatial Redis** — use Redis GEO (`GEOADD`/`GEORADIUS`) so riders query "drivers within 1 km" directly against the cache, never touching the DB. (c) **Pub/sub fan-out** — driver writes publish to a Redis channel; riders subscribe to their region and get push updates. Uber's actual design uses Redis GEO + pub/sub, with the DB as a periodic checkpoint for crash recovery.
**Visual:**
```
Cache-aside (BAD for driver location):
write every 4s -> DEL cache  -> next read misses -> DB -> SET cache
                                       ^^^^^^^^ DB hit every read cycle

Write-through (BETTER):
write every 4s -> SET cache + DB write  -> read always hits cache (fresh)
```

### Q6. YouTube's video metadata cache uses cache-aside with a 1-hour TTL. A creator edits the title; viewers still see the old title for an hour. Fix without sacrificing hit rate.
**Answer:** The TTL is the staleness bound, but writes should also invalidate the cache so the new title appears immediately. Add a write-path invalidation: when the creator edits the title, the metadata service updates the DB and then `cache.del(video:{id})` so the next read fetches the fresh value. This makes the staleness window "until next read" instead of "until TTL expires" — typically under a second. The 1-hour TTL remains as a safety net in case the invalidation fails (network blip, Redis down). To prevent the stale-then-overwrite race, use delayed double-delete or versioned keys (`video:{id}:v{version}`). For multi-region deployments, propagate invalidations via a Pub/Sub channel (Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka) so all regional caches invalidate within seconds. Finally, for the CDN edge cache (which serves the rendered HTML page), use a separate invalidation API (Cloudflare/Akamai purge by surrogate key) so the edge doesn't serve stale HTML either. Net effect: viewers see the new title within ~1 second of the edit, hit rate stays at 99%+, and the 1-hour TTL only kicks in if invalidation fails. YouTube uses roughly this design with surrogate-key-based CDN purges.
**Visual:**
```
Without write invalidation:        With write invalidation:
creator edits title                 creator edits title
DB updated                          DB updated
cache still has old title           cache DEL video:42
(viewers see old for 1 hour)        next read: miss -> fresh DB -> repopulate
                                    (viewers see new within ~1s)
                                    TTL=1h stays as safety net
```

### Q7. You're caching API responses for a public weather API. Clients expect fresh data every 10 minutes. Cache-aside with a 10-minute TTL causes periodic stampedes. How do you fix this without breaking the freshness SLO?
**Answer:** The SLO is "data is at most 10 minutes old," not "data refreshes exactly every 10 minutes." Several fixes that preserve the SLO: (1) **TTL jitter** — set TTL to 10 minutes ±1 minute random; expirations spread out, eliminating synchronized stampedes. Data is at most 11 minutes old, which is acceptable if the SLO is interpreted as "approximately 10 minutes." (2) **Refresh-ahead** — set TTL to 12 minutes, but a background worker refreshes each key at the 10-minute mark; readers always hit a fresh cache (≤10 minutes old), and the worker absorbs the DB load off the read path. (3) **Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch)** — set TTL to 12 minutes, but each read after the 10-minute mark probabilistically triggers a background refresh; this spreads refreshes across requests naturally. (4) **Stale-while-revalidate** — set TTL to 10 minutes, but on expiry serve the stale value for up to 2 minutes while a background refresh runs; data is at most 12 minutes old. (5) **Per-key coalescing** — when the cache misses, only one request fetches; others wait. Combining jitter + refresh-ahead + coalescing gives 99%+ hit rate, no stampedes, and data freshness within the 10-minute SLO.
**Visual:**
```
Naive: TTL=10min, all keys expire together -> stampede every 10 min

Fixed:
  TTL = 10 min +/- 1 min jitter        (expirations spread)
  refresh-ahead at 9 min               (read path always hits)
  per-key coalescing on miss           (1 fetch per key)
  --> 99%+ hit rate, no stampede, data <= 10 min old
```
